html:
The mita, or mit'a in Quechua, was a system of turn-based labour service in the Andes. The Inca Empire used it to run the state, and the Spanish later turned it into a forced labour draft for their mines.

Under the Inca, each household owed the state turns of work rather than taxes in goods. Men served as soldiers, built the roads and terraces, farmed state and temple lands, and carried loads. Officials counted the work on quipu knotted cords, and the state fed workers from its storehouses. The Inca built on older Andean customs of shared work.

In the 1570s the viceroy Francisco de Toledo reshaped it for the Viceroyalty of Peru. Each year about one adult man in seven from a wide area of the highlands had to go to the silver mines of Potosí, and others to the mercury mine of Huancavelica. Peoples such as the Qhara Qhara and Sora were drafted. Pay was low, the work deadly, and many families fled their villages to escape it. As the encomienda faded after the New Laws of 1542, the mita became the main form of forced labour in Peru.

Túpac Amaru II demanded its end in his rising of 1780. The Spanish parliament at Cádiz abolished it in 1812.
